<explanation>
1. Identify the project type and purpose  
   - This is a full-stack Elixir/Phoenix application (lib/algora + lib/algora_web) with an integrated GitHub App and payment processor.  
   - Business logic lives in `lib/algora` (contexts: accounts, activities, bounties, chat, payments, workspace, etc.). The web UI and API are in `lib/algora_web` (LiveView, controllers, components).  
   - Static content and docs are in `priv/content`. Asset building uses Node.js + Svelte + Tailwind (assets/). Background jobs use Oban.

2. Analyze the file structure  
   - Top-level directories:  
     • assets/ → front-end build (Svelte components, TS, CSS, JS)  
     • config/ → environment configs for dev/prod/test  
     • lib/algora/ → core contexts and domain logic  
     • lib/algora_web/ → Phoenix endpoint, router, controllers, LiveView, components, plugs  
     • priv/repo/ → Ecto migrations & seeds  
     • rel/ → release scripts (Distillery or Mix releases)  
     • test/ → ExUnit tests for contexts, web, integrations  
   - Key config: `Dockerfile`, `fly.toml`, `.env.example` for external service keys (GitHub, Stripe, S3, Cloudflare Tunnel).  
   - Background work: Oban jobs in multiple contexts (activities/jobs, bounties/jobs, workspace/jobs, etc.).

3. Examine the README for additional insights  
   - Describes three “apps” in one codebase: Web app, GitHub App, Payment engine.  
   - Uses Docker/Postgres in dev, external dependencies: GitHub webhooks & polling, Stripe webhooks, S3 for static assets, Cloudflare Tunnel for local webhooks.

4. How to draw an accurate system design diagram  
   a. Main components  
      - Client (Browser)  
      - Asset build pipeline (Node/Svelte/Tailwind)  
      - Phoenix Web Server (algora_web)  
      - Domain/Context layer (algora)  
      - Database (Postgres + Ecto)  
      - Background Workers (Oban)  
      - GitHub Integration (API clients, Webhook endpoint, Poller)  
      - Stripe Integration (Webhook endpoint, SDK)  
      - Static Asset Storage (S3 bucket)  
      - Tunnel Service (Cloudflare Tunnel/ngrok)  
   b. Relationships & interactions  
      - Browser ←→ Phoenix (HTTP requests + WebSocket for LiveView)  
      - Phoenix → Postgres (Ecto queries)  
      - Phoenix → Oban → Background jobs → Postgres  
      - Oban jobs → External APIs (GitHub, Stripe, Email, etc.)  
      - Webhook endpoints (e.g. `/webhooks/github`) ← Cloudflare Tunnel ← GitHub/Stripe  
      - Asset build → Docker image → served either by Phoenix or uploaded to S3  
   c. Architectural patterns  
      - Phoenix MVC + LiveView for UI  
      - Contexts (separation of domain logic)  
      - Supervisor tree (Application.ex starts endpoint, Repo, Oban, Poller supervisors)  
      - Async job processing with Oban  
      - Behavior-based adapters for external services (e.g. GitHub behaviour)  
   d. Key technologies  
      - Elixir/Erlang (OTP)  
      - Phoenix Framework (LiveView, Controllers, Plugs)  
      - Ecto + Postgres  
      - Oban for job queues  
      - Node.js toolchain (pnpm, Svelte, TS, Tailwind)  
      - GitHub API & Webhooks  
      - Stripe API & Webhooks  
      - AWS S3 (or S3-compatible)  
      - Cloudflare Tunnel/ngrok for local testing  

5. Tailoring the diagram for this full-stack app  
   - Draw the browser/UI layer at the top, label LiveView vs. static assets.  
   - Immediately below, show the Phoenix endpoint → router → controllers & LiveViews → contexts.  
   - Group individual contexts into one “Domain Layer” box but call out Oban workers as a sub-box.  
   - Show the Postgres database box with an arrow from both the Domain Layer and Oban.  
   - Place external integrations (GitHub, Stripe, S3) around the Phoenix/Domain box, with arrows indicating API calls and webhooks.  
   - Add a small “Tunnel” box between Webhook sources and Phoenix in dev.

6. Diagram styling guidelines  
   - Use clear, distinct shapes:  
     • Rounded rectangle – Client & external services  
     • Rectangle – Internal services (Phoenix, Domain)  
     • Cylinder – Database  
     • Cloud icon – Tunnel or S3  
   - Color code layers:  
     • Green for UI/Client  
     • Blue for Phoenix & Domain  
     • Orange for Background Workers  
     • Gray for Database  
     • Purple for External Services  
   - Label every component and connection.  
   - Use directional arrows to show data flow (requests, webhooks, background jobs).  
   - Group related modules (e.g. all `lib/algora/activities/*` under “Activities Context”).

7. Emphasize detail but avoid clutter  
   - Include every major context only if it clarifies data flow (e.g. Accounts, Bounties, Chat can be sub-contexts).  
   - Highlight core paths: user login, bounty creation, tip sending, job application, webhook handling, payment flow.  
   - Annotate the Oban queue with examples of jobs (send_email, notify_discord).  
   - Call out the Poller supervisor under GitHub integration to show event-driven vs. webhook flows.

By following these guidelines, the principal engineer can craft a diagram that clearly articulates how the Phoenix application, contexts, database, background jobs, and external integrations collaborate to deliver Algora’s web, GitHub App, and payment‐processing functionality.
